cells.tense: You are tending something that is growing at its own pace, and your hands are not forcing it.
cells.act: surrender the outcome and keep the act
cells.ask: Keep every part of the care you already give it. Release only the ending — decide, plainly to yourself, that how it turns out is not yours to hold — then keep tending anyway, however it goes.
cells.core:
Something in your care is coming up at a pace you didn't set, and you're letting it. You water, you wait, you don't pull on the stem. That's not passivity — it's why the thing is taking root instead of just obeying you. When a wall comes down here, it comes down because it couldn't hold, not because you tore it down. You're standing near a clearing you didn't have to make.

The release in this is earned, not forced. What you're gripping can be put down because a stretch of work is finished, not because you quit. So name the outcome you keep reaching for — say it once, to yourself — and hand it over. Keep every part of the care, release only the ending. That's the whole move. It's small, it's daily, and it leaves your hands free for whatever wants to grow next.
cells.sheetLine: Growth is happening and your hands aren't forcing it.
cells.place: where a structure built on a false premise comes down

cells.tense: You are going to run past what you are tending, and the care is already turning into control.
cells.act: take the next step with only enough light for that step
cells.ask: This week, before you tend it, name what you actually know — no more — take one step from that, then wait. Don't arrange today to match how you picture the finish.
cells.core:
The next thing gets planned before it's grown here. You can see the version that turns out well, and you're arranging today to match that picture — checking, adjusting, keeping the whole finish in your head. Care that can't wait starts to press on the thing it's tending, and on the people near it. The clearing you want is a wall coming down by itself; bracing for its arrival is how a new one gets built.

So work from what you've lived, not from what you're imagining. This week, before you tend it, name what you actually know — no more — take one step from that, then wait. Sketch the whole of it badly on one page if that helps, keep the sketch, and don't demand the finish before the first step.
cells.sheetLine: The planning has gotten past the thing it's for.

cells.tense: You cared for what needed tending, and the want that used to pull you forward has gone quiet.
cells.act: remember what drew you and face it again
cells.ask: Think of something you'd be sorry to lose, and give it five minutes that plainly face it. Don't wait to feel like it first — the feeling comes after the turning.
cells.core:
Care keeps going out from you to people and things, and almost nothing grows back in this part. You've stayed capable, independent, fine on your own — and that's done well enough that nobody notices what it costs. Something you'd once have said you wanted is still there and hasn't been named in a long time. Wanting it again isn't a failure of your independence.

Think of something you'd be sorry to lose, and give it five minutes that plainly face it. Don't wait to feel like it first — the feeling comes after the turning. What's been starved gets fed by that turning, not by forcing yourself to care harder. Aim at one light before you sort out the whole sky.
cells.sheetLine: You care for everything but what you'd be sorry to lose.

cells.tense: You are holding things up in this clearing that nobody actually assigned you, and you call it helping.
cells.act: stop holding what no longer serves
cells.ask: Choose something you keep up mainly because it would fall if you let go. Let it — tell whoever it concerns, or just leave it. Then keep your hands free a while.
cells.core:
People bring things to you and set them down, and you keep them up. In this clearing you're what things lean on, and nobody wrote that down anywhere — including you. If someone asked, you'd say you just help. All of it is a job, and the job has a keeper. The clearing already took away some false structures, and one that remains is the one where this is all your responsibility by default.

Choose something you keep up mainly because it would fall if you let go. Let it — tell whoever it concerns, or just leave it. Then keep your hands free a while. Not forever; long enough to feel the weight gone. Whatever really needs you will come back and ask.
cells.sheetLine: You're what things lean on and nobody asked you.
cells.place: where a structure built on a false premise comes down

attempts.check: The unsupported claim in the Too Little draft is that the person withdrew from something or that nothing ever grew — the record only says the seat is running on empty and the block is chronic, so the cell must say where the person stands (care given out with nothing growing back, wants not named) and not what happened there or who, how long ago, what it cost. A reader could reasonably say 'I haven't withdrawn, I just haven't found the thing yet' — the ask still works for them, because naming the one they'd be sorriest to lose and facing it costs nothing and teaches them something either way. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any version of 'you give more than you get' as a general fact — it's flattering to the card, so it's dropped. Also slots four: the exact act is 'put it down and leave your hands empty a while' — NOT 'set it down', which is another card's exemplar language; the asked object must be something the person is gripping, not a newborn or a seedling, or the Nurturing card would be prescribing itself.
